CI/CD workflows invoking tools (e.g., gomplate) with postExec that access environment secrets and perform network exfiltration
Workflows triggered on pull_request_target with write permissions and access to sensitive environment variables
file_indicators: .gomplate.yaml with postExec section executing shell commands
main.tf containing local-exec provisioner with network command invocations
main.tf using http provider with suspicious or non-standard URLs
.github/workflows/* referencing documentation formatting tools with shell command execution
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to attacker-controlled domains such as attacker.example.com during terraform apply or CI/CD workflow execution
Requests containing sensitive data (e.g., tokens, state files) as URL parameters or POST data
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Terraform modules and CI/CD workflows for use of local-exec provisioners that invoke network commands, http provider blocks with non-standard or attacker-controlled URLs, and workflow files that run documentation formatting tools with postExec hooks. Flag any access to sensitive environment variables (e.g., GITHUB_TOKEN) combined with outbound network requests. Alert on the presence of .gomplate.yaml files with postExec sections executing shell commands, and on workflows triggered by pull_request_target that grant write or secret access. Correlate outbound network activity to known attacker domains and inspect for exfiltration of sensitive data.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the code checks environment variables against a large filter list of known sandbox, CI/CD, and analysis environment indicators, and aborts further execution if any are detected, enabling sandbox and automated analysis evasion.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of a comprehensive filter list targeting known sandbox and CI/CD environment variables, combined with conditional logic to abort execution, is a well-known evasion technique used by malware to avoid detection during automated analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not attempt to detect or evade sandboxes or security analysis environments. Such behavior is only seen in malware or highly targeted attack tools.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, some software may check for CI/CD or test environments to adjust non-malicious behavior, but not to evade detection or prevent execution.
key_indicators: Large filter list of environment variables associated with sandboxes and CI/CD systems
Conditional early return to avoid execution in analysis environments
Obfuscated or programmatically constructed filter entries

package_info.why_malicious: Multiple versions of the package exfiltrate all environment variables to an attacker-controlled webhook, use obfuscated and dynamically constructed hostnames, and implement sandbox evasion techniques to avoid detection. The latest version (0.1.0) is benign to bypass security scanners, while the majority of versions are malicious and designed for dependency confusion attacks targeting build and CI/CD environments.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed as a dependency due to dependency confusion, leveraging high minor/patch version numbers to supersede internal packages.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code execution on the victim machine

attack_chain.action: On import or runtime, the code checks environment variables for known sandbox, CI/CD, or analysis indicators to evade detection.
attack_chain.leads_to: If not a sandbox or analysis environment, proceeds to data exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Collects all environment variables from the victim machine using process.env.
attack_chain.leads_to: Prepares sensitive data for exfiltration

attack_chain.action: Exfiltrates the collected environment variables to an attacker-controlled webhook using a POST request to a dynamically constructed subdomain.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive credentials and secrets from the victim environment

behavioral_signatures: Access to process.env and exfiltration of all environment variables to external domains
Network POST requests to dynamically constructed subdomains of pipedream.net at import-time or runtime
Conditional logic to evade sandboxes or CI/CD environments based on environment variable checks
Obfuscated or programmatically constructed hostnames and filter lists in JavaScript code
file_indicators: build.js containing both process.env access and http.request usage
Obfuscated or minified code in non-production npm packages
Presence of large, programmatically constructed filter lists for environment variable checks in build.js
network_indicators: *.m.pipedream.net
POST requests to subdomains such as eoxb1lay4m45mms.m.pipedream.net
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that access all environment variables and send them to external domains, especially at import-time or during installation. Flag packages with obfuscated or dynamically constructed code, large environment variable filter lists, or network requests to known exfiltration domains such as *.m.pipedream.net. Use both static and dynamic analysis to inspect all package versions, not just the latest, and correlate build.js file contents with suspicious network activity.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime during schema parsing, the code evaluates the contents of the user-supplied schema file using eval with restricted builtins, directly processing attacker-controlled input, resulting in arbitrary code execution if the schema is malicious.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Passing unsanitized user input to eval is a well-known code injection vulnerability, as it allows attackers to execute arbitrary code. Even with restricted builtins, attackers can often bypass these limitations using Python's introspection features.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Schema validation should only parse and check schema definitions for correctness, not execute code from user-controlled files. Using eval on untrusted input violates this expectation and introduces severe risk.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use of eval may occur in tightly controlled environments for evaluating safe, internal expressions, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input such as schema files.
key_indicators: Direct use of eval on user-controlled input
Attempted but insufficient restriction of builtins
No input sanitization or whitelisting of schema content
Schema file content is executed as Python code

execution_context.file_location: parser.parse (internal function, called when validating a schema file)

package_info.package_versions: prior to the fix for CVE-2021-38305
package_info.why_malicious: Yamale is vulnerable to arbitrary code execution because it passes unsanitized user input from schema files directly to Python's eval() function. This allows attackers to inject and execute arbitrary Python code by supplying a malicious schema file, resulting in a critical security risk when used in untrusted environments.

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains control over the schema file supplied to Yamale (via -s/--schema parameter).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious payload is placed in the schema file.

attack_chain.action: Yamale parses the schema file and passes its contents to eval with restricted builtins.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code in the schema file is evaluated.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code in the schema file executes arbitrary Python code (e.g., system commands, network actions).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker achieves code execution on the victim system.

behavioral_signatures: Use of eval on user-controlled schema files during validation
Schema files containing Python code or suspicious reflection patterns (e.g., __class__, __bases__, __subclasses__)
Execution of system commands or network actions during schema validation
file_indicators: Schema files with __import__, __class__, __bases__, __subclasses__
Schema files containing system command strings such as 'os.system', 'subprocess.Popen', or 'http.server'
network_indicators: Unexpected outbound network connections initiated during schema validation
Unusual HTTP server startup or reverse shell activity originating from the validation process
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for use of eval on schema files within the Yamale package, and scan schema files for suspicious Python code patterns such as reflection (__class__, __bases__, __subclasses__), __import__, or system command invocations. Alert on unexpected process creation or network activity during schema validation. Use static analysis to flag schema files with code execution patterns, and enforce the use of ast.literal_eval or strict whitelisting for any dynamic evaluation of schema content.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime during terraform apply, the code uses the http provider to send sensitive values extracted from the Terraform state to an external server via HTTP POST, resulting in state data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code sends sensitive data from the Terraform state to an external server, which is a clear exfiltration attempt and a violation of infrastructure-as-code security best practices.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Terraform modules should never transmit state data or secrets outside the controlled environment or to untrusted domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: The http provider is sometimes used for legitimate API calls, but it should not be used to send secrets or state data to external, non-approved endpoints.
key_indicators: Use of http provider to POST data to external domains
Inclusion of sensitive values from Terraform state in HTTP request body
Outbound network requests to attacker-controlled URLs
No legitimate business justification for external data transfer

package_info.package_versions: unspecified (all versions prior to commit SHA pinning mitigation)
package_info.why_malicious: The module enables arbitrary code execution through the local-exec provisioner and the http provider, both of which can be abused to exfiltrate sensitive data such as environment variables, secrets, or Terraform state. Additionally, a vulnerable GitHub Actions workflow allows attacker-controlled code execution during documentation formatting, leading to credential theft and potential repository hijack. These behaviors violate the expected security boundaries of Terraform modules and CI/CD workflows.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits a pull request or modifies the module to include malicious local-exec or http provider code in main.tf.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is merged or published in the Terraform Registry, making it available to users.

attack_chain.action: User or CI/CD pipeline runs terraform apply, triggering execution of the malicious local-exec or http provider code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive environment variables or Terraform state data are exfiltrated to the attacker's server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits a pull request with a crafted .gomplate.yaml file to exploit the documentation formatting workflow in GitHub Actions.
attack_chain.leads_to: GITHUB_TOKEN is exfiltrated, enabling the attacker to push tags or further compromise the repository.

behavioral_signatures: Terraform modules using local-exec provisioner to run shell commands that access environment variables or secrets
Terraform modules using http provider to POST sensitive data (such as secrets or state values) to external, non-corporate domains
CI/CD workflows running gomplate with untrusted .gomplate.yaml files containing postExec commands that perform network exfiltration
Workflows triggered on pull_request, pull_request_target, or untrusted code paths that access secrets or environment variables
file_indicators: main.tf with local-exec provisioner referencing environment variables or secrets
main.tf with http provider sending data to domains not on an allowlist
.gomplate.yaml with postExec containing curl or other network commands
.github/workflows/* referencing gomplate or executing user-controlled templates
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., https://attacker.com/exfil) during terraform apply or CI/CD runs
HTTP POST requests containing environment variables, secrets, or Terraform state data in the payload
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Terraform modules for use of local-exec provisioners and http providers that access or transmit sensitive data, especially to non-approved domains. Audit CI/CD workflows for use of template engines (such as gomplate) that execute user-controlled postExec commands, particularly when workflows are triggered by pull requests or untrusted code. Flag any outbound network requests from terraform apply or CI/CD processes to domains not on an allowlist, and review workflow and template files for patterns that enable arbitrary code execution or secret access. Implement automated scanning for these indicators to prevent credential or data exfiltration.
